description: Overpass is looking for 1 to 3 teammates for the MODIS/VIIRS Hot Spots challenge (Universal Event). Open-source, science-first. Need: data/stats, web or 3D (Three.js), and someone who loves clear writing and design. Reply with your time zone and what you’d like to own.
summary: We built Overpass, which is a web app based on a python pipeline that joins NASA's satellite fire records into one record running from November 2000 to today. Terra and Aqua MODIS, Suomi VPP VIIRS and NOAA-20 VIIRS all count fires different. VIIRS can see more small fires, which causes the record to jump in 2012 even though the land itself did not change. Overpass functions as a currency converter. For each hand off between satellites, it learns an "exchange rate" from the years when two satellites flew together, then converts every month into one shared unit, S-NPP fire days. It tries five models, from one simple factor all the way up to quantile mapping, and keeps the simplest one that holds up on years it wasn't fitted on. Every converted month has a 90% range. Step tests at each hand-off and single satellite checks make sure a sensor change can't pass for climate trend. The app shows a 26 year fire calendar, this month compared properly against past years, and fire season timing, and all the data downloads for any region. This matters now because Suomi NPP stopped sending fire data on Nov 2, 2026. Without harmonization, land managers, scientists, and reporters can't tell if it is a real change in fire, or a change of camera.
details:
People judge a fire season by comparing it with past ones. Is this year worse than 2005? Are fires getting more common here? NASA's satellite fire record should answer that, but it was built by different cameras in turn. MODIS on Terra and Aqua flew first with 1 km pixels. VIIRS on Suomi NPP took over in 2012 with 375 m pixels and sees far more small fires. So the record jumps when the camera changes, not when the land does. In the ten regions we built, raw fire counts rise 2.5 to 5.6 times at the 2012 hand-off. Put the records end to end and you see a crisis that never happened.

It just happened again. Suomi NPP stopped sending fire data on 2 November 2026, and NOAA-20 now carries the record. That makes three camera changes, and the latest came two weeks before this hackathon.

Overpass works like a currency converter. When two satellites flew at the same time, they watched the same fires, so we can learn the exchange rate between them. Overpass learns that rate for each hand-off and converts every month into one unit: what Suomi NPP VIIRS would have counted. Terra and Aqua are calibrated on 2012–2020, when they flew alongside S-NPP, and NOAA-20 on 2020–October 2026. For each hand-off, five models compete, from one global factor up to quantile mapping, and each is scored on years it wasn't fitted on. Every converted month carries a 90% range.

A python pipeline does the work in 9 stages.

1. Fetch - Download data from NASA FIRMS

2. Clean - Keep vegetation fires only, drop volcanoes and industry heat sources

3. Grid - Put each detection in a 0.25 degree square on its local solar date

4. Aggregate - Sum per month, and flag satellite outages

5. Calibrate - Fit conversions

6. Validate - Test on held out years

7. Clock - Measure fire season timing and Aqua's orbit drift

8. Nowcast - Compare this month with the same days of past years

9. Export - Write JSON and CSV for the app

The unit is the fire day, which is one grid square with fire on one day.

The web app turns this into something anyone can read using React, Type Script, and Vite.

The sections of our site are described below:

Calendar: 26 years on one grid (raw and harmonized)

This month: Compares days 1 to d of this month with days 1 to d of past years, so a half finished month doesn't look abnormal

Season: Is the fire season starting earlier or lasting longer? A trend is only a trend if the stats support it, and it is rechecked on a single camera so a satellite change can't pass for a climate change.

Evidence: Shows every test, including the ones where the method failed

Scenes: Cliff Melt shows the record as 3D terrain whose 2012 cliff flattens when harmonized. Column Flyover flies over a region one grid at a time.

We wrote down what we expected before looking at the results, then tested each claim on real data across 10 different regions on 6 continents, Córdoba, California, Portugal, Punjab–Haryana, Zambia, Central Kalimantan, Southeast Australia, Mato Grosso, Alberta and Central Sakha.

- The jump is gone: After harmonizing, the 90% interval for the 2012 step includes no change in all 10 regions

- Two cameras check each other: Terra and Aqua, converted separately, agree with 11% on 2002-2011 totals in every region.

- We report what failed: NOAA-20 reads 1–7% higher than S-NPP, so it needs its own conversion. Interval coverage falls short of 90% in four regions, and a leftover break near 2012 can't be ruled out in Central Sakha. The app flags each one.

Benefits and intended impact:

Overpass keeps NASA's fire record going past the end of Suomi NPP. Every fire record built on S-NPP now needs a bridge to NOAA-20, and Overpass already has one that has been tested. It also makes 26 years comparable. Land managers, fire scientists, insurers and journalists can compare 2003 with 2023 without mistaking a camera change for a change in fire. Every converted number carries a range, and every claim links to the test behind it, so users know how far to trust what they see. The tool runs on free NASA data.

How it is creative:

The core idea is an everyday metaphor. Calling the conversion an "exchange rate" turns a calibration problem into a sentence a reporter can repeat. Behind that metaphor, complexity has to earn its place. Five models compete on years they never saw, and the simplest winner is kept, which in Mato Grosso turned out to be a single global factor. Where we could measure something instead of quoting it, we did. Aqua's orbit drift, about 100 to 130 minutes later by 2026, is measured from the overpass time stamped on every detection. We also made failure part of the product: the Evidence view shows the checks the method failed next to the ones it passed. Finally, the fix is something you can watch. The Cliff Melt scene shows the 2012 cliff in the raw record flattening into one smooth surface as it is harmonized.

Factors we considered:

The first decision was what to count. Raw pixel counts reward sharper cameras, because one fire can light up dozens of VIIRS pixels, so we count fire-days: one grid square with fire on one day. Dates got the same care. UTC splits one afternoon's fire across two calendar days in much of the world, so every detection is placed on its local solar date. Satellite outages would look like quiet months, so they are flagged and left out of fitting. The current month is compared with the same days of past months, never with whole months, so a half-finished month doesn't look unfairly low.

We designed for everyone who might use it. The color scale, cividis, reads the same for people with color-vision deficiency. The typeface, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, was designed for low-vision readers. The app is also built to be reliable and fast. Finally, we were clear about scope: Overpass is a research and communication tool, and it does not replace local fire authorities.

Tools used:

Languages - Python 3.11 and Typescript

Pipeline - NumPy, pandas, PyArrow, scikit-learn, PyYAML, requests, pytest

Web App - React 19, Vite, d3, three.js, deck,gl, MapLibre GL JS, Vitest

Hosting - Vercel

Development - Github, SI (described in readme linked below)

Hardware - Our own laptops
